prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "BANK OF AMERICA CORP /DE/" (ticker BAC), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BAC", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Bank of America Corporation
markets: Credit and debit cards and payments
Wealth management and brokerage (Merrill, Bank of America Private Bank)
Commercial and corporate banking and treasury services

mission.statement: At Bank of America, we are guided by a common purpose to help make financial lives better through the power of every connection.
mission.source: Bank of America company profile and careers materials (company purpose statement)
mission.plain: Bank of America wants to help people and businesses handle their money better by connecting them with what they need.

about.plain: Bank of America is one of the biggest banks in the United States. People keep their money there in checking and savings accounts, use its debit and credit cards, and borrow from it to buy homes and cars. Through Merrill it helps families invest and save for retirement. It also lends to and advises big companies and helps them buy and sell stocks and bonds.
about.customers: Tens of millions of ordinary people and small businesses, wealthy families, and large companies, governments and investment funds.
about.everyday: If you have tapped a Bank of America debit card, used its Erica app assistant, or sent money with Zelle from its app, you have used its products.

money.plain: checking and savings accounts, cards, home and car loans
investment advice and accounts for families
loans, payments and deal advice for companies
trading stocks, bonds and currencies for big investors
app-based banking and AI assistants that sell more products digitally

result.summary: Bank of America has a real but mostly scale-based advantage: it holds about $2.0 trillion of deposits, is No. 1 in US consumer deposits, and its low-cost, sticky checking accounts fund lending more cheaply than most rivals. Its combination of a national branch and digital network with Merrill wealth management creates cross-selling and switching costs, but banking products are largely commoditised and its returns (14.2% ROTCE in 2025) trail JPMorgan's.

pricingPower.evidence: It pays below-market rates on a large base of checking deposits (total deposit rate 1.49% in Q3 2026) while still adding about 680,000 net new checking accounts in 2025 and over 200,000 in Q3 2026 (31 straight quarters of growth), but loan, card and trading prices are set by competitive markets and a proposed $5 debit fee had to be dropped in 2011 after customer backlash.

moats.evidence: Bank of America and Merrill are household names, and Bank of America ranked #31 on Fortune's 2026 World's Most Admired list, but the brand is less of a draw than JPMorgan's and was damaged by mortgage-crisis scandals and the 2026 $1.2B anti-money-laundering penalty.
Moving direct deposits, bill pay, cards, mortgages, Merrill accounts or a company's CashPro treasury systems is painful; 64% of Merrill/Private Bank clients also bank with it, deepening the tie.
Some benefit from payments scale (it co-owns Zelle operator Early Warning Services) and trading liquidity, but a new customer does not make the bank much more valuable to other customers.

With $113.1B of 2025 revenue, $2.04 trillion of deposits and about 3,600 financial centers it spreads compliance and technology cost over a huge base, and its low-cost deposits cut its funding cost below that of smaller banks.
Only a handful of US banks (JPMorgan, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citi) have national deposit franchises plus global investment banking, and heavy capital rules deter new entrants.
It is the incumbent; fintechs, neobanks and private-credit funds counter-position against it rather than the reverse.

Its 'responsible growth' discipline and digital execution (Erica, 50 million active digital users, 71% of consumer sales made digitally in Q3 2026) are hard to copy, though the 2026 OCC and FinCEN consent orders show gaps in compliance processes.
Merrill's large adviser force and $5.1 trillion of wealth client balances, plus a national branch network, would take decades to replicate.

customers.evidence: It has posted 31 straight quarters of net checking account growth through Q3 2026, 11.4 million clients in its Preferred Rewards loyalty programme (Q4 2025), and about 21,000 net new Merrill/Private Bank relationships in 2025, though consumer reviews of big banks are typically mixed.

talent.evidence: It has been on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For eight years running through 2026, ranked #10 on LinkedIn's 2026 Top Companies in the US, and raised its US minimum wage to $25 an hour in 2025.

product.evidence: Its digital banking and Erica assistant are widely regarded as industry-leading and it is No. 1 in US consumer deposits, but it ranked #3 in investment banking fees in 2025 (Dealogic) and trails JPMorgan in cards and trading.

threats: Compliance and regulatory risk: a $1.2B non-tax-deductible penalty under OCC and FinCEN consent orders over anti-money-laundering and sanctions failures (October 2026), with consent orders that can restrict activity
Falling interest rates: a 100bp drop in the forward curve would cut about $1.9B from 12-month net interest income, its largest revenue source
A recession lifting card and commercial real estate credit losses

ceo.name: Brian Moynihan
ceo.background: Lawyer; Brown University AB in history, University of Notre Dame JD; former FleetBoston executive; also chairman

c1.evidence: Retail and investment banking is a mature industry; Bank of America's revenue grew about 6% a year from 2022 to 2025.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for convenience (about 3,600 financial centers, 50 million active digital users, the Erica assistant) and Preferred Rewards perks tied to Merrill balances; scale and switching costs last, but products are easy for big rivals to match.

c3.evidence: The name is recognised by almost every American and it is No. 1 in US consumer deposits, but JPMorgan Chase, not Bank of America, is generally seen as the default leader, and big banks rarely earn enthusiastic recommendations.

c4.evidence: It repeats its purpose 'to help make financial lives better through the power of every connection' and its 'responsible growth' mantra, but the mission is generic for a bank and management is judged mainly on profit and returns.

c6.evidence: “big, convenient, bureaucratic, fees” — the brand is seen as safe and everywhere but impersonal, and memories of the 2008-era mortgage scandals and fees, plus the 2026 $1.2B anti-money-laundering penalty, make the impression mixed rather than mostly positive.

c7.evidence: US banking and wealth management are huge markets (it alone holds about $2.0 trillion of deposits and $5.1 trillion of wealth client balances) but they grow roughly with the economy and wealth rather than riding a fast secular trend.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into new US cities with branches and growing wealth and AI-driven digital sales, but regulation and its 10%+ US deposit cap on acquisitions limit big new markets.

m1.evidence: Moynihan has a clear, consistent strategy of 'responsible growth' and early digital investment (Erica launched 2018), but he is seen as a steady operator rather than a visionary.

m2.evidence: Not a founder, but he has run the bank since 2010, says he will stay through the end of the decade and has emphasised long-term, steady growth over quick profits.

m4.evidence: Under Moynihan the bank raised its US minimum wage to $25 an hour (2025), paid about $6.8B of Sharing Success awards to employees since 2017 and made eight straight Fortune 100 Best Companies to Work For lists.

m5.evidence: He built a disciplined, risk-aware culture with strong digital innovation (Erica, CashPro, AI tools used by over 200,000 employees), but it is not known for inventing new products and technologies at a fast pace.

m6.evidence: Moynihan is a lawyer by training (Notre Dame JD), not an engineer, and leads as a general manager rather than hands-on with technology.

m7.evidence: He is respected for steady stewardship, community investment and employee pay, but his record includes the 2011 debit-fee backlash, rising pay ($41M for 2025) and the compliance failures behind the 2026 $1.2B penalty.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Moynihan at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or a similar top university was found; he became Chancellor of Brown University in July 2024.

m8b.evidence: Moynihan is known as a low-key, disciplined executive (a former Brown rugby co-captain), not a larger-than-life public personality.

m9.evidence: He rebuilt the bank after the 2008 crisis (selling 23 non-core businesses in his first six quarters), grew net income from $17.9B in 2020 to $30.5B in 2025, and was named Chief Executive magazine's CEO of the Year in 2020.

m10.evidence: The bank runs a long-standing expense discipline and kept headcount flat at about 213,000 in 2024-2025, but its 2025 efficiency ratio was about 62% and Moynihan's company-jet commuting has drawn criticism.

c10.evidence: It safely holds savings, payments and loans for tens of millions of US households and businesses, but its reach is mostly American and its services are essential utilities rather than life-changing products.

p2.evidence: Running a $3.4 trillion balance sheet safely under heavy regulation is hard and important to the economy, but the core products are similar to those of other large banks.

f1.evidence: Revenue net of interest expense rose every year from $85.5B in 2020 to $89.1B (2021), $95.0B (2022), $102.8B (2023, revised), $105.9B (2024, revised) and $113.1B in 2025.

f2.evidence: Pre-tax margin rose from 22.2% in 2020 ($19.0B on $85.5B) to 33.3% in 2025 ($37.7B on $113.1B), but 2020 was depressed by pandemic reserves and banks report no gross margin.

f3.evidence: Shareholders' equity was positive at $296.7B in September 2026, but like all banks it uses heavy leverage, with $380.9B of short-term borrowings and long-term debt against $249.6B of cash and cash equivalents.

f4.evidence: Pre-tax income rose from $19.0B in 2020 to $37.7B in 2025 though it dipped in 2022, and bank operating cash flow swings widely with trading and balance-sheet moves.

v1.evidence: Its accounts and cards are good and its Erica app is well regarded, but JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo and others offer very similar products, so there is no single practical reason to pick it over every alternative.

v2.evidence: It has made Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For eight years in a row through 2026 and ranked #10 on LinkedIn's 2026 Top Companies list for the US.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, tens of millions of depositors, Merrill clients and businesses would lose their accounts and loans and the financial system would be shaken, but other big banks could take over its services over time.
